summary.text:
Bexley's 2025/26 outturn is the first paper in the library where we hold both sides of the same trade. Appendix B lists temporary borrowing of £5m from Herefordshire County Council at 7.00%, 26 March to 27 April 2026; Herefordshire's own outturn, published to a different committee two months earlier, lists the matching 32-day deposit with the London Borough of Bexley at 7.00%, maturing 27 April. Principal, rate and maturity date agree exactly.

That loan is one of five. All £25m of short-term borrowing was struck between 24 February and 26 March and matures in the first half of April, at a weighted 5.97% — Bridgend and Hastings at 6.00%, Herefordshire at 7.00%, Redbridge 5.35%, London Treasury Liquidity Fund 5.50%. It sits on top of a £224.584m PWLB book costing 3.34% while £10.149m of investments earned 4.11%.

The loan book ties to our file to the pound: 87 loans, £224,583,813, weighted 3.3369%. So does their EIP repayment figure — two semi-annual instalments of £15,625 against the stated £0.031m. CFR £318.59m less external borrowing £249.58m less other long-term liabilities £26.36m leaves £42.65m of internal borrowing, consistent with their own statement that existing loans are insufficient to meet the projected CFR.

One presentational point worth recording: Table 6 is headed 'PWLB New Loan Certainty Rate' and every figure in it is 20bp above the certainty rate for that day — that is, it is the standard rate. Their own glossary defines the 20bp gap correctly. On the DMO's curve today the book carries about £61.5m of net discount, the largest we have computed, because 78 of 87 loans sit well below the current curve.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the outturn report that went to General Purposes and Audit on 29 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. We hold 87 PWLB loans for Bexley totalling £224,583,813 at a weighted 3.3369%, against the £224.584m at 3.34% in your Table 4a — to the pound and to the basis point. Your EIP figure ties as well: PW497847 runs semi-annual instalments of £15,625, two of which fell in the year, which is the £0.031m in your 3.10. Add the £6.000m of maturity repayments and you get the £6.031m movement exactly. Table 5a foots and every percentage in it recomputes, as does the Appendix A maturity structure once the £25m of short-term borrowing is included.

We wrote because of something we have not been able to do before.

Your Appendix B lists temporary borrowing of £5m from Herefordshire County Council at 7.00%, drawn 26 March and maturing 27 April 2026. Herefordshire's own 2025/26 outturn went to their Cabinet on 21 May, and its investment table lists a 32-day fixed term deposit with the London Borough of Bexley at 7.00%, £5.00m, maturing 27 April 2026. Same principal, same rate, same maturity date, and 26 March to 27 April is 32 days. Two councils, two committees, two months apart, describing one loan from opposite ends.

We mention it because it is the first time we have been able to see a single inter-authority trade from both sides, and it makes a point neither report can make alone. From where you sit, that £5m is one of five loans at a weighted 5.97%. From where Herefordshire sits, it is one of four deposits that helped turn a £0.552m investment budget into £2.534m of income. The same trade is a cost line in one set of papers and a windfall in the other, and neither authority can see the distribution it sat in.

That distribution is the reason we track this. Across everything we have read this year, inter-authority pricing over this year end ran from 4.45% to 8.50% — Lancashire, Suffolk and West Northamptonshire lending at 4.45-4.50% in the same quarter that Cornwall paid Blackburn with Darwen 8.50% for four days and Harlow paid 7.75% for a month. Your five loans at 5.35% to 7.00% sit in the upper half of that, which is unremarkable for money struck in the last five weeks of March: the year end concentrates hard dates, and hard dates are what produce the spread. July's PWLB lending was thin at £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, and thin PWLB months are when the inter-authority market prices widest. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

The second thing is your Table 6. It is headed "PWLB New Loan Certainty Rate", and the five figures for 31 March 2026 — 5.92, 6.43, 6.49, 6.50 and 6.28 — are each exactly 20 basis points above the certainty rates for that day, which were 5.72, 6.23, 6.29 and 6.08 on the four tenors we hold. Twenty basis points is the gap between the standard rate at gilt plus 100 and the certainty rate at gilt plus 80, and your own glossary sets it out correctly: "It allows councils to borrow at 20 basis points (0.20%) below the standard rate." The 31 March 2025 row runs 20bp high on the same pattern. So the table is the standard rate under a certainty heading, and the year-on-year increase it shows is real either way. It makes no difference to anything you did — you did not borrow long in the year — but it is the sort of thing that quietly sets the wrong reference point when a future report compares a drawn rate against it. For what it is worth, today's certainty rates on notice 314/26 are 5.83% at ten years and 6.38% at twenty.

Third, the break-cost position, because it has moved a long way from where your book was struck. On the DMO's premature repayment curve this afternoon, 78 of your 87 loans price below par, for about £61.5m of net discount against £2.6m of premium on the other nine — the largest net discount we have computed for any council. It is what a £224.6m book at 3.34% looks like against a curve in the mid-fives. The single largest is the £8.5m at 1.86% running to 2069, at roughly £5.0m. The largest premium is the other end of the same history: £5m drawn in October 1996 at 8.00%, maturing September 2056, carrying about £1.77m.

We're not suggesting anything follows from that. We don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote a real figure. The reason it is worth a line at all is that your 3.15 says officers will draw longer-term debt when it becomes favourable, and the £42.65m of internal borrowing implied by your CFR of £318.59m against £249.58m of external debt and £26.36m of other long-term liabilities is the size of the decision that sits behind that sentence. Yours is priced daily at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On training, four fit Bexley. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets and LA Credit Analysis go to the £25m of year-end money. PWLB explained covers the rate bases behind Table 6, and PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator covers the discount position above. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell

Source: Annual Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025/26, General Purposes and Audit Committee, 29 July 2026. Herefordshire figures from their Treasury Management Report 2025/26, Cabinet, 21 May 2026.
